questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
questions.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-{y}^{2}={z}^{2}$ at the point $(2,0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-{y}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2})k \\  & =\frac{x}{2}\text{ }i-2y\text{ }j-2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,0,1) & =\frac{(2)}{2}\,i-2(0)\text{ }j-2(1)\,k \\  & =i-2\,k \\  & =⟨1,0,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(2,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(2,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨2,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(2,0,1)=⟨2,0,1⟩+t\,⟨1,0,-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=xy+5x+{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =(y+5)\text{ }i+x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(-1+5)\,i+(1)\,j+2(2)\,k \\  & =4\,i+j+4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $4\,i+j+4\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
questions.problem: Consider the plane curve ${y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}=4xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,-3).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2} & =4xy \\ {y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,-3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy)\,j \\  & =(6x-4y)\,i+(2y-4x)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,-3) & =(6(-1)-4(-3))\,i+(2(-3)-4(-1))\,j \\  & =6\,i-2\,j \\  & =⟨6,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,-3)=⟨6,-2⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(-1,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{6} & =\frac{y-(-3)}{-2} \\ (-2)(x+1) & =6(y+3) \\ -2x-2 & =6y+18 \\ 6y+2x+20 & =0 \\ 3y+x+10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(0,0,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z)\,k \\  & =({e}^{x+y+z}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{x+y+z}+1)\text{ }j+({e}^{x+y+z}+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,0,0) & =({e}^{0+0+0}+1)\,i+({e}^{0+0+0}+1)\,j+({e}^{0+0+0}+1)\,k \\  & =2\,i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $2\,i+2\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $4xy+2{x}^{2}=x+2y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side: 

$$
\begin{aligned}4xy+2{x}^{2} & =x+2y \\ 4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y)\,j \\  & =(4y+4x-1)\,i+(4x-2)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(4(-1)+4(2)-1)\,i+(4(2)-2)\,j \\  & =3\,i+6\,j \\  & =⟨3,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨3,6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{3} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{6} \\ 6(x-2) & =3(y+1) \\ 2(x-2) & =y+1 \\ 2x-4 & =y+1 \\ 2x-y-5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$
